```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(geomfeliscatus)
```

This vignette walks through the pieces that make `geom_cat()` work.  It is
a map of the extension points, in the order you need them when you write
your own geom.

## A layer is a Geom, a Stat and a position

Every `geom_*()` and `stat_*()` function builds a layer.  A layer needs
three collaborators:

- a **Geom**, which turns data into graphical objects (grobs),
- a **Stat**, which computes on the data before it is drawn, and
- a **position**, which adjusts the data after the stat.

`geom_cat()` uses the identity stat and the identity position: the data
goes in unchanged and each row becomes one cat.

```{r}
GeomCat
```

The class name is CamelCase and the `geom_*()` function is snake_case, so
`GeomCat` pairs with `geom_cat()`.

## Step 1: declare what the geom needs

A `ggproto()` object inherits from `Geom` and declares a handful of
fields:

```{r eval = FALSE}
GeomCat <- ggproto(
  "GeomCat",
  Geom,
  required_aes = c("x", "y"),
  non_missing_aes = c("size", "coat"),
  default_aes = aes(
    coat = "black",
    size = 8,
    colour = NA,
    fill = NA,
    alpha = NA,
    linewidth = 1,
    angle = 0
  ),
  extra_params = "na.rm",
  draw_key = draw_key_cat,
  draw_panel = function(self, data, panel_params, coord,
                        eyes = "open", whiskers = TRUE, seed = 1) {
    # ...
  }
)
```

- `required_aes` are checked before drawing and produce the familiar
  "requires the following missing aesthetics" error.
- `default_aes` are filled in for aesthetics the user did not supply.
  Anything listed here is also an aesthetic, so `coat`, `size` and
  `angle` can be mapped in `aes()` or fixed in the `geom_cat()` call.
- `non_missing_aes` are removed when missing, like `size` here.
- `extra_params` lists parameters that are not aesthetics but are accepted
  by the layer, such as `na.rm`.
- `draw_key` draws the legend key.

Notice that `eyes`, `whiskers` and `seed` are formal arguments of
`draw_panel()`.  That is what makes them valid layer parameters: ggplot2
collects a geom's parameters from the arguments of `draw_panel()`.

## Step 2: turn data into grobs

`draw_panel()` receives the layer data, the panel's scales and the
coordinate system.  The first job is to transform the data to npc
coordinates (0 to 1 within the panel):

```{r eval = FALSE}
coords <- coord$transform(data, panel_params)
```

The result has one row per cat and columns for every aesthetic, after
scaling.  A pictogram geom then draws one grob per row.  `geom_cat()`
gives each cat its own viewport, sized in millimetres:

```{r eval = FALSE}
grid::gTree(
  children = do.call(grid::gList, grobs)
)
```

Inside `cat_grob()` the cat is drawn in a square coordinate system from 0
to 1, so the drawing code never has to think about the panel's shape.  The
viewport does that work:

```{r eval = FALSE}
grid::viewport(
  x = x, y = y,
  width = width, height = height,
  angle = angle,
  clip = "off"
)
```

Two grid details are worth remembering:

- `gpar(lwd = )` is measured in 1/96 inch, not millimetres.  `geom_cat()`
  converts the `size` aesthetic to a line width so that outlines scale with
  the cat.
- **Sibling grobs must not share a name.**  `grid` only draws the first of
  several siblings with the same name, so the layer's gTree is left
  unnamed.  Inside one cat the parts are named (`"cat_body"`, `"cat_head"`,
  ...) so tests can find them; the sticker border copies get a `.halo`
  suffix so they do not collide with the coloured part.

## Step 3: draw the legend key

A legend key is just a small grob.  `draw_key` receives the key's data, the
layer parameters and the key size, and draws in a 0 to 1 viewport:

```{r eval = FALSE}
draw_key_cat <- function(data, params, size) {
  cat_grob(
    x = grid::unit(0.5, "npc"),
    y = grid::unit(0.5, "npc"),
    width = grid::unit(0.9, "snpc"),
    height = grid::unit(0.9, "snpc"),
    coat = data$coat %||% "black",
    # ...
    stroke = 0.9 * (data$linewidth %||% 1)
  )
}
```

`"snpc"` units are square npc units: the cat stays square even when the
legend key is not.  Without a `draw_key`, the legend would use the default
`Geom` key, which draws nothing useful for a cat.

## Step 4: write the user-facing function

The `geom_*()` function is boilerplate.  Copy the shape of
`ggplot2::geom_point()`: the geom is fixed, the stat is flexible, and
everything else goes into `params`.

```{r eval = FALSE}
geom_cat <- function(mapping = NULL,
                     data = NULL,
                     stat = "identity",
                     position = "identity",
                     ...,
                     eyes = c("open", "closed"),
                     whiskers = TRUE,
                     seed = 1,
                     na.rm = FALSE,
                     show.legend = NA,
                     inherit.aes = TRUE) {
  eyes <- match.arg(eyes)
  layer(
    geom = GeomCat,
    stat = stat,
    data = data,
    mapping = mapping,
    position = position,
    show.legend = show.legend,
    inherit.aes = inherit.aes,
    params = list2(
      na.rm = na.rm,
      eyes = eyes,
      whiskers = whiskers,
      seed = seed,
      ...
    )
  )
}
```

The `...` is what makes `geom_cat(coat = "calico", size = 12)` work:
`coat` and `size` are aesthetics, so ggplot2 moves them from `params` into
the layer data and recycles them to the number of rows.

## Step 5: custom aesthetics and their default scale

`coat` is not an aesthetic ggplot2 knows about.  That is fine: any name in
`default_aes` becomes an aesthetic.  When the user maps it, ggplot2 looks
for a default scale by name.  For a discrete aesthetic called `coat`, it
looks for `scale_coat_discrete()` in the environment of the `ggplot()`
call.  That is why the package provides one:

```{r eval = FALSE}
scale_coat_discrete <- function(..., guide = "legend") {
  scale_discrete_identity(aesthetics = "coat", ..., guide = guide)
}
```

An identity scale is the right choice here because the values *are* the
coats: `"tuxedo"` is a recipe for drawing a tuxedo cat, not a colour.
If you invent an aesthetic whose values need translating, return a palette
from a `discrete_scale()` instead.

## Step 6: test the pieces

Testing an extension has three layers of its own:

1. Test the data preparation and the drawing helpers directly.
   `coat_spec()` is a pure function, so its output is easy to assert.
2. Test the layer through ggplot2.  `ggplot_build()` gives you the
   render-ready data, and `layer_grob()` gives you the grob:

   ```{r}
   plot <- ggplot(data.frame(x = 1:3, y = 1:3), aes(x, y)) + geom_cat()
   grob <- layer_grob(plot)[[1]]
   length(grob$children)
   ```

3. Test the errors with snapshots, so the whole message is reviewed:

   ```{r eval = FALSE}
   expect_snapshot(error = TRUE, match_coat("dalmatian"))
   ```

Visual regression tests (for example with `vdiffr`) are a good addition
for a geom whose whole job is appearance.

## Step 7: package plumbing

An extension package needs very little beyond a normal package:

- `DESCRIPTION` lists `ggplot2` in `Imports`.
- The package-level doc block imports ggplot2 and the grid functions you
  use, and roxygen writes `NAMESPACE`.
- Every exported function and ggproto object has documentation.
- `devtools::document()`, `devtools::test()` and `devtools::check()` are
  the loop.

`GeomCat` is exported so that other packages can build layers with it, and
so that `layer(geom = GeomCat, ...)` works in examples and tests.

## The local scaffold

This repository ships the scaffolding used to develop the geom:

- `dev/preview.R` renders every coat to `dev/output/` for a quick visual
  check.
- `inst/templates/geom-template.R` is a commented template with a Geom, a
  Stat, a scale and a `draw_key`.
- `dev/README.md` describes the edit, preview, test, document loop.

Copy the template into a new file with:

```{r eval = FALSE}
usethis::use_template(
  "geom-template.R",
  save_as = "R/geom-mything.R",
  package = "geomfeliscatus"
)
```

- `vignette("extending-ggplot2", package = "ggplot2")` is the official
  reference for the Geom and Stat APIs.
- The [ggplot2 book](https://ggplot2-book.org/ext-ggplot2.html) chapter on
  extending ggplot2.
- [Easy geom recipes](https://evamaerey.github.io/easy-geom-recipes/), a
  gentle, example-first route through Stats and geoms.
- The [ggplot2 extenders club](https://ggplot2-extenders.github.io/ggplot-extension-club/),
  a community of people building extensions.
